utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-R77.2, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I'm barrister from Canada appearing as amicus curiae Prosecutor in these proceedings, and with me this afternoon and throughout the proceedings is Lori Ann Wanlin, also from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Good afternoon, Mr. Seselj. For the record, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Vojislav Seselj, professor -- university professor and the accused in The Hague with the longest detention -- time in detention in the history of courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you're following this procedure in the language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If at any time you have a problem, please let us know. Well, the Trial Chamber indicated in its order of 22nd of May the trial in this case will be held today. Before the -- we start the trial, there are a couple of matters to be dealt with as part of Pre-Trial Conference, so first is a planning of the trial. Mr. MacFarlane, how long do you expect your Prosecution case to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the trial will consist essentially of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, could you turn on your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the case for the Prosecution essentially will have two main components. The first is the tendering, physical tendering of a series of documents; and the second will be the submission with respect to those so that they're in context. There will be no witnesses, so my best assessment is that the case for the Prosecution will be in the vicinity of three hours or thereabouts. Most of that, I should say, will involve my submission to the Chamber with respect to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, I don't follow in full. You need three hours to submit the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No. I -- perhaps I could be clearer on that. The actual physical --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should be a bit clearer on that. The actual physical tendering of the exhibits probably won't take much more than a half an hour or so. It is the submission with respect to the evidence, in essence the closing submission that will require the bulk of my time. So what would normally be the tendering of the evidence will be relatively short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the -- what would the other time be composed of in terms of three hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I expect I will need about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would include the opening statement and closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you think your opening statement would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It would be relatively brief. I expect it would be ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then before we go on -- move further, why don't we deal with your -- the motion for admission of exhibits from the bar table. As we indicated in our previous order, we'll deal with it now orally. Do you have anything to add in addition to what is stated in your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The -- the legal framework and the submission is contained within that material. There wasn't anything further that I was going to add. I was simply going to reaffirm what I've already said in the motion document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was not clear to me is the -- is the book, the -- it's 65 ter number 1 refers to the B/C/S version, and number 2 refers to the English translation. Am I correct in so understanding? And your intention is, then, to tender the whole book in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No. No, it's -- no, it's not my intention to tender a physical book. The -- what will be tendered is a hard copy in English and B/C/S of the relevant portions of the book, but the physical hard copy book with a cover will not be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The -- one category of documents you are planning to tender are the documents from the main trial case, as well as in present case to which Chamber, you, and the accused have access and which is part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need to tender them as exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I will be referring to them, and they in turn will have linkages to the translation of the book so that it -- it seemed to me that having them as part of the record would be preferable. I recognise that they form part of the overall record of the Tribunal, but it seemed to me and it's my submission that having them before you so that you can compare and contrast certain parts of it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me hear from Mr. Seselj. My understanding is that the translation of the motion has been disclosed to you yesterday. Is it correct, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would first of all like to tell you that I'm going to insist upon my right to use an equal amount of time as the Prosecutor is going to use, but I have an objection to the request by the Prosecutor that he needs three hours. I consider that that is much too much and that he can present everything in a much shorter space of time so that the trial can be completed today. And I think that it is in the general interest to save time whenever possible, especially since this is not the main trial, and I have to deal with more important matters. Now, with respect to the request made by the Prosecutor that these documents be tendered into evidence, it is true that it was only yesterday that I received the translation of that list of documents, and a few days ago I received a pile of other documents, but I have managed to get through all of them, so I'm not make -- I'm not going to make any objections. And the third thing that I wanted to tell you is this: It is highly problematic to ask that documents be directly entered into evidence in this way. However, bearing in mind the fact that here we're dealing with generally known documents, at least it is common knowledge to this Tribunal, I'm not going to object to that either, because I think there's no reason for me to object to documents for which it is a notorious fact that they are in existence. So that would be unreasonable. It would be unreasonable to object. But I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that there are too many documents which are not needed and which encumber and burden the list. Many things are not being challenged from the outset. It is -- I'm not challenging that I'm the author of the book. So there's no need to prove that on the basis of documents. I have said that a number of times. I have also explained during the main proceedings the way in which I compiled the book and gave instructions for the book's printing. So we would have to discuss matters here which are contentious, and what is contentious is whether there was disclosure of protected witnesses at all or not. And then the question of motivation comes into play. What my motives were. Were my motives to disclose the names of protected witnesses or to unmask a plot in public with respect to (redacted) that is incorporated into my indictment for which there is to legal grounds, and I think that is the substance of the matter and the essential question. So I have nothing against having evidence -- having admitted into evidence that three witnesses enjoyed protective measures and that I was informed on time that they were in fact protected witnesses and that I knew that their names could not be disclosed. That can be admitted into evidence straight away. There's no reason for me to challenge that at all and oppose it. So that's a whole set of documents here which the Prosecutor has attached. Then, furthermore, I have nothing against having all the transcripts from the main trial be admitted into evidence and my comments about the book and the portions where I explain how the book came into being in the first place, and we have documents here testifying to the publication of the book and its public promotions in Serbia. I have nothing against that either. I don't object to that being admitted into evidence, and if I'm not contesting it, then why? And here we have statements which were made by these protected witnesses on several occasions. Now, is that necessary? Do you need to tender that into evidence I leave it up to you to weigh that up. I think that this once again burdens the whole subject matter. The only problem, in my opinion, is this: It is that from the available documents I concluded that the book was not translated in its entirety, that only sections and excerpts have been translated, and I consider that nowhere in the world can a serious court be able to try and pass judgement in a matter of this kind without being provided an insight into the entirety of the book. And I'm convinced, Judges, gentlemen, that you cannot understand the entirety of the book on the basis of just some excerpts and sections from the book. And let me remind you of what the famous French Cardinal Richelieu once said, and he said, Just give me one sentence from any text and I'll find sufficient reasons to send the author to the gallows. That would not be serious. It wouldn't be a serious trial and case. So why then did the Prosecutor not ensure that you had the entire book translated? Last time the Prosecutor gave you incorrect information to the effect that the book was 1.400 pages long. The book is just 1.200 pages long, which means 200 pages less, 200 pages less to translate, and the Prosecutor had enough time at his disposal to provide you with the comprehensive translation of the book, because you'll be able to understand the book only if you read it from cover to cover. And when I come to give my opening statement, I will explain to you what the contents of the book is. But on the basis of the Prosecution's position and my explanations, but without you having read the whole book, I don't think you'll be able to try this case. If you believe otherwise then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, if you could explain us -- explain to us the relevance or necessity to tender those witness statements, whether you can live without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The charge against Mr. Seselj specifically refers to disclosing portions of the statement of one of the witnesses. That's very much a part of the charge. And with respect to the other two witnesses, some portions of the statement are not just disclosed but they disclose what I'll refer to as identifier information as well. So for all of those reasons, the statements do form a part of the landscape on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything you'd like to respond to Mr. Seselj's argument that whole book should be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, there are a few things I would like to say. First of all, with respect to the length of the book, Mr. Seselj has in court today the hard copy with the cover, and it's my understanding that that is 1.200 pages. The downloaded web site version is 1.400 pages and that was the version that we were using. That's the answer for the 1.200 versus the 1.400. In terms of the translation of the full book versus the relevant portions, as I mentioned on the last occasion, we had a translator go through the entire book and it became evident, as that person was going through it, that the vast majority of the book is completely irrelevant. It deals with matters that are far away from the issues before this Chamber, so that those portions of the book that are relevant, either identify or tend to identify, are the portions that have been translated formally. In context we erred on the side of translating probably a bit too much to ensure that there was context. Yet, at the end of the day, it became largely an issue of the amount of time that would be required to have a formal translation of a book that was 1.400 pages long with very dense word capacity. So that was also a matter that was taken into account given the fact that contempt proceedings are intended to be relatively straightforward and expedited. Those are all the factors that were taken into account in ensuring that the relevant portions of the book were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. MacFarlane. If the -- this bar table motion is to be dealt with during the course of Pre-Trial Conference, so to speak, now, there would be no need to separate opening statement and closing argument, or you can do it in one batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd be quite happy to do that, Your Honours, and in fact depending on how the proceedings unfold this afternoon, it may well be that I could expedite my comments in such a way that I wouldn't require the number of hours that I mentioned. It might be less than that. I recognise the desirability of dealing with the matter as the accused has pointed out today, and I will endeavour to do whatever I can to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to come to you. Do you like to say something beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope, Judges, that you have noticed something very important in the statement that the Prosecutor has just made. The Prosecutor said that in the book there are elements which could identify the witnesses. So he's now uncovering the essence of the case. There are certain elements which could identify, he says. Probably there are, but neither -- the Prosecutor did not dare say that I, in fact, identified the names of protected witnesses, because the identification must be clear and direct if that is to be stated and not to be understood. It might be understood in certain parts, but how are you going to look at the motives of the publication of this book - that's the question - if you haven't got an insight into those parts which the Prosecutor says are irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, that's a matter for the trial. We'll come to those issues very briefly when trial starts. For the planning purpose, I'd like to know what kind of evidence you are going to -- you plan to tender today. I take it you are not planning to propose any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since the Prosecutor hasn't planned any witnesses, I don't plan any either. Had the witness had -- had the Prosecutors had witnesses, I would have had five witnesses of my own, and I've already proofed them. But since the Prosecutor won't bring any witnesses forward, I won't either, but I do consider that the entire book must be admitted into evidence and on the list, because without it this trial would have no sense. To try me for a book which you don't have in its entirety, I think that would be totally unacceptable and impermissible. And the Prosecution, the OTP, received a copy of the book from me. I gave it to them personally, and they can have it dealt with in a short space of time. I don't know why the Prosecutor in this case has not been given a copy of the book. I suppose they're so interested in the book and find it such fascinating reading that they couldn't leave it out of their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you have other exhibit to tender than the book in question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing more than that. No, I'm not going to propose anything else, to tender anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds the exhibit tendered by the amicus curiae Prosecutor relevant and of probative value and therefore we -- we admit it -- admit them in their entirety. But those material which may reveal the protected, confidential information will be put under seal. I will not deal with item by item, but with the assistance of the registrar that will be communicated to the parties. And coming to your book, Mr. Seselj, we will admit it in its entirety into evidence. However, that does not necessarily mean the whole book should be translated. Those relevant parts and necessary parts can be referred to in the course of trial by you, which means those parts can be translated, and if necessary, the Chamber will look into the parts that may be raised during the course of trial later on. That said, it is for you, Mr. MacFarlane, to open the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The first order of business probably would involve the tendering of the exhibits and their marking, or does the Chamber have another approach in mind in terms of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to this request by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this Prosecutor's request. Since I never contested any of these documents proposed by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber can automatically, without any objection on my part, admit them into evidence, and based on the supporting request from the OTP assign only one number to it, but it can also give it identical sequential numbers contained in the Prosecution request for the sake of saving time. My impression is that the Prosecution wants intentionally to waste time on this. I think that one sentence based on the agreement of both parties will provide a solution to this issue. I thought that we can move on to the essence of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you, Mr. Seselj. Those have been tendered, admitted, disclosed, the numbers can be assigned later on and communicated to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm certainly anxious that the proceedings move expeditiously. I was going to suggest that one way to approach it would be to have the numbers that are set out in the annex to my motion, have those accepted as the exhibit numbers and that could be achieved very quickly and not -- during the course of a break or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be done easily. I would like to check with the registrar whether there's any problem with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Mr. MacFarlane is kindly requested to speak into the microphone to his right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, you can proceed on that basis. The -- your numbers are identical in both 65 ter motion and the bar table motion? You used the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not clear about this. I have an Annex A and an Annex B and they did at one time appeared to be identical but for the reference to the book. Now, is one of them what I should be viewing as the index of numbers of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My suggestion is that we use the confidential Annex B to the motion which is headed "Contents of CD using the Rule 65 ter Exhibit Number." So that's Annex B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Annex B includes on the face of it the whole B/C/S version of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And that would accommodate the accused in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it -- there's -- yes. So it's on the second page with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that gets round any issue over admitting the book. It's part of your -- the documents that you tender. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a couple of comments before I move into the evidence per se. This is, in my respectful submission, a relatively straightforward case. It involves a publication contempt allegedly of the Tribunal. There's one accused, one charge, and one publication. What makes the case a bit different is that the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, if you could speak into the microphone. One thing I forgot to mention both to you and Mr. Seselj is that to avoid the information that may reveal the identity of the protected witnesses, and then I'd like to remind Mr. Seselj again of the fact that the title of the book is -- is under seal, so not to mention the exact title of the book in the open court. So when necessary, we may go into private session. Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll endeavour to ensure that I'm being recorded and translated. What -- what sets this case perhaps off to the side in a different way from other cases is that the evidence will demonstrate that the accused embarked on a course of conduct with a view to camouflaging the identification of the witnesses, with a view to avoiding criminal proceedings, and in his view, the evidence will demonstrate that he felt that only a clever person would be able to figure out the identification of the witnesses. It's my submission on the evidence that identification is open to any reasonable person with knowledge of the facts and that just about anyone could figure out the identification in the book. And as well, the accused has been relatively open about his plan in this particular case. And that takes me -- that takes me into the trial transcripts. These are the transcripts from the main trial. Not all of the transcripts will be necessary for me to make reference to because of the admissions made by the accused. The -- the issue of the promotion of the book, the accused has already commented on that. I would just simply note that the -- a couple of transcripts are relevant. The first one that I would draw to the attention of the Chamber is on the 7th of May, 2009, page 29. The accused notes that not only is he the author of the book, that he's very proud of it, and thanks to these legal proceedings there's been a lot of interest in the book on his internet site. Several thousand copies have been photocopied and reproduced and that he was very satisfied. That addresses the question of the scope of the publication of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I think I'll leave it at that point. There's other transcripts dealing with the promotion and the scope of the publication, but with a view to expediting proceedings, I would simply note (redacted) (redacted) distributed, that in Belgrade at the trade union building during one of the promotions there were approximately 3.000 people present. And I think I'll leave it at that in terms of scope of publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Some portions of the transcripts are relevant, in my respectful submission, to the issue of mens rea, and there's two -- two transcripts in particular. The first occurred on the 9th of October, 2008, at page 10.582. The accused said in essence this:

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: (redacted) That is the fruit of their labour pursuant to my instructions. They are my extended arm in all of this." That indicates the nature of the relationship between the advisors on the team and the accused. The advisors and the team appear to have largely prepared it but pursuant to the instructions as an extended arm of the accused. A similar comment was made by the accused on the 21st of October, 2008, at pages 10.810 and 10.811. To make sure that it's seen in context I'll read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, sorry to interrupt you, but can I remind you to try not to reveal the information that may reveal the title of the book, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to steer around some words. The accused is reported as having said this: "Now, in addition to this (redacted), that is great deal of mystification on the basis of this book and it's a report that my associates compiled for me as an attachment for my last complaint against the indictment. You know, the text was a letter lengthy one, about 300 pages, and you ordered that it should not be translated into English. I said it should be printed and published but that the names be thrown out and that the code-names be used, the codes used by the Prosecution, and in that book you'll see those codes." And then he continued. "Now, the fact that someone who is clever and intelligent can draw their own conclusions as to who the person is, well, what do I care about that?" And it's that last comment that I submit is particularly relevant to the question of mens rea. It appears that the accused issued instructions, recognised that clever and intelligent persons may be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker go a bit more slowly when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, when you read the text could be more slower for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could repeat from when you said: "It appears that the accused issued instructions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I will repeat that relevant portion, Your Honours. "And it is a report that my associate compiled for me as an attachment for my last complaint against the indictment. You know the text was a rather lengthy one, about 300 pages, and you ordered that it should not be translated into English. I said it should be printed and published but that the names be thrown out and that code-names be used, the codes used by the Prosecution, and in that book you'll see those codes." And then the accused continued in a particularly important way. "Now, the fact that someone" -- pardon me -- "somebody who is clever and intelligent can draw their own conclusions as to who the person is, well, what do I care about that?" The further comments that are relevant to the issue of mens rea, Your Honours, it appears that the accused made a conscious decision to avoid in particular one particular witness's name, and he gave specific instructions to avoid that name. I will be dealing with that, because if you look through the textbook, it becomes apparent that even that person can be identified. This is in essence a jigsaw puzzle that the accused and his associates endeavoured to put together to defeat any criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: On another occasion -- I'll be drawing my comments to a conclusion on the transcripts in just a moment. On the 25th of February, 2009, at page 14.261, the accused made this comment with respect to the book in question: "In my case, in a beautiful book, 1.200 pages, with a lovely title, in the introductory remarks I never revealed the names of protected witnesses, and in the appendix to the book, in various documents that I've gathered, you can find documents where full names are indicated of witnesses, but you don't get to have their pseudonyms right next to those names, so you really have to put in an effort, and you have to be quite smart in order to perhaps be able to divine the identity of those witnesses." In my respectful submission, that's a particularly telling excerpt from the transcript on the issue of mens rea. His plan was to ensure that nowhere is the pseudonym and the real name together on the same line or in the same area of the book, and on my review of the book, it appears that he was pretty successful in doing that, but that was the plan. So he said, "We never put them together, so you really have to put in an effort, and you have to be quite smart in order to perhaps be able to divine the identity." And as we go through the book, I will be submitting to the Chamber that that's essentially the nature of the book. He was successful in terms of avoiding placing the pseudonym and the name of the witness together, but by virtue of context and content and activity, anyone with a reasonable intellect can figure out who the witnesses are. There is one final comment I have with respect to the main trial transcripts, but of necessity I'll need to deal with protected information, so we might want to move into closed session for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means. I don't -- private session will be sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just -- yes, we are now in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In the event of a finding of guilt on the count, following are my submissions with respect to the appropriate sentence. There's quite a range of fact situations when it comes to publication contempt, from what -- what some might characterize as low-level publication contempt straight through to attempts to interfere with witnesses and in some cases intimidate witnesses or in essence scare them off. So there's many different scenarios that can arise. In my submission, these three witness had very tight protection which was provided by the Chamber. It was apparent to the Chamber that they needed protection, and the steps that were taken were very serious. I guess that's point number one. The second point is that it's become apparent that the accused embarked on a deliberate course of action. He deliberately camouflaged the -- or endeavoured to camouflage the names of the witnesses so that he could put his book out, and at the same time, anyone who took a look at the book, read the book, would understand who the witnesses were and in that sense exposed them to the world, because the world can read the book on the accused's web site. So scope is clearly an issue. The protections around the witnesses is an aggravating feature. This is clearly an attempt to try to manipulate or intimidate the witnesses by exposing them. The accused contends that he didn't intimidate. I submit to the Chamber that that's not accurate. This was an attempt to intimidate and to expose them despite the protective measures imposed by the Chamber. I've had occasion to review virtually all of the contempt cases from 1999 to 2008, and in some instances a monetary penalty was imposed, in other instances a term of imprisonment, anywhere between 3, 4, and 5 months has been imposed by the Chamber. It's my respectful submission that in the facts of this case, where carefully protected witnesses have been exposed through a concocted plan, the upper range of penalty is called for to make it clear that the Chamber will not tolerate this sort of manipulation and subterfuge with a view to exposing a witness that has been manipulated. It's my submission that a term of imprisonment is called for and that it ought be on the upper range as being appropriate on the facts of the case. So those are my basic comments on the question of sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Mr. Seselj, now it's your time to present your case to the Chamber as well as any evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, at the beginning I have to admit to you that I'm very unpleasantly surprised by the presentation of Mr. MacFarlane, his appearance as amicus curiae of the court. I had expected a more competent and more professional approach. He is a man -- he was expected to be a man who would provide a full insight into the case and accusations, and thereafter, to prove that there was an existence of crime, and then after that he would have been expected to prove that there was intent or mens rea. He did neither. His approach was a theological [as interpreted] one, which means it was targeted. Please correct the transcript immediately. Here it says "theological," whereas I said "teleological," and your interpreters are not properly educated to know the difference between "theological" and "teleological." It just occurred to me at this moment to look at the transcript because I have very bad experience with the interpreters that you have here. So therefore, he had a very focussed and targeted approach. He was interested in collecting pieces of evidence that could support the indictment. Raw extraction of the arguments from the context of the book can -- appears to be supporting his allegations and charges, but basically this is clouding the key point. He has not read the book and is unable to give an assessment of the book, whereas he says that the motive behind the publishing of this book was to disclose the names of the witnesses. Had he read the book, he could never have arrived at this conclusion. Let us make a little experiment. In order for me to prove to you that Mr. MacFarlane has no idea, absolutely what this book contains? For example, he doesn't know how many times the name of Mr. Ian Bonomy, the member of this Trial Chamber, appears in the book. He doesn't know that because nobody told him so. You see, look how he's wriggling in his chair, his body language and his look shows that he doesn't know. The name of Judge Bonomy has been mentioned in this book four times because Judge Bonomy was a member of the Trial Chamber which I addressed on several occasions with respect to certain procedural and legal issues, and for that reason his name is included in the cover pages of four documents. This brings us to the question how this book came about. The Trial Chamber II that was conducting pre-trial proceedings against me until the beginning of 2007, deprived me of the right to file an appeal to the second amended indictment for some procedural reasons including even the deadlines for filing such motions. For that reason I appealed to Trial Chamber III and presented the problem of failing to file an appeal, and I requested a new deadline. The Pre-Trial Chamber III -- and you can find all these documents at the beginning of the book, and the Prosecutor should have informed you about that. Trial Chamber III, sometime in October 2007, granted me a new deadline to file an appeal against the indictment, and I did that. The motion was compiled by my legal associates, and I attached to it a 300-page supporting document. In this analysis I wanted to provide to the Trial Chamber abundant evidence that would force them to eliminate one part of the indictment against me as completely unfounded. I suppose that Judge Parker remembers 2004, when he was member of the Trial Chamber conducting preliminary phase. In 2004, the Trial Chamber of which he was a member deliberated on my preliminary motion against the indictment. Among several locations mentioned as one that were related to the charges of crimes, one location should have been removed from the indictment unless the Prosecution had any proof that there was -- there was a war conflict going on on that specific location. The Appeals Chamber included again this portion into the indictment by simply announcing that the burden of proof of whether there was an armed conflict or not is on the trial; that is to say, that during the trial the case should be put forward to prove or disprove whether the war was going on or not. However, I had sufficient evidence to say that there was not only no war, but there was no attack even. You know that according to Rule -- to Article 5 of the article, in order for it to be implemented, in addition to a war, it provides for the existence of an attack that has to be widespread or systematic. I provided quite a few pieces of evidence in this study that there was no attack, and there was no systematic or widespread attack even more. Reynaud Theunens from the OTP confirmed in the courtroom that there were no attacks launched against the civilian population in those specific locations. However, what happened at that point? The Trial Chamber was impatient and was under the pressure of the Council of Europe who had been demanding for a trial against me to start as soon as possible, without all the requirements being fulfilled, didn't have time to deal with this study. They even instructed this study not to be translated. And the trial was scheduled out of the blue, without all procedural requirements being fulfilled. All the evidence, according to 65 ter were not disclosed to me. The decisions concerning all interlocutory motions were made. In a nutshell, not everything was in place for a trial to start according to the rules. In such circumstances, I decided to publish this study of mine, and I issued strict instructions to my associates not to mention in this study the names of the protected witnesses, which is stated in the preface to the book. In the study, which is from 477 -- actually, from 77 to 330 and something page - I have no time now to look for it - not a single name of a protected witness is mentioned, but all their statements have been refuted as false. I would like to bring to your attention that there are such incredible statements. For example, that at the rallies of the Serbian Radical Party I publicly advocated the killing of all the children from mixed marriages, and other monstrous things. You know, I have already published a 1.000 book [as interpreted] called "The Hague Instrumentalisation of False Witnesses," which contains a huge number of witness statements who gave statements, false statements, under the pressure from the Prosecution but refused to appear live. Please do not go into private session, because this has nothing to do with this trial. This book was mentioned on many occasions during the main trial. In addition to this -- the publication of this study, I also gave instructions for all the documents that we managed to get hold of be published, which indicates the true nature of the events that were taking place in this specific location mentioned in the indictment. I am not mentioning the name of the location. This contains interviews with people who were, in a certain way, involved in these events, as well as interviews with members of the state security service, police, local residents. There are also statements given to the police, police information, and court papers. Through this voluminous documentation, which contains 900 pages, I have portrayed virtually everything that happened in this location, literally everything. Nothing was omitted. The three witnesses mentioned here were public figures by virtue of their offices or their profession. They were well known in their community, and it was impossible in this other portion of the documentation to avoid the mentioning of their names and their involvement in certain events. I had no right, as far as the documents that we provided through research on the ground, I had no right to intervene with what they contained or to falsify them in any way. They were put in proper order and published as such. When the Prosecutor said -- when -- when the Prosecutor says that a witness can be identified on the basis of the contract on swapping flats, he extracted only one portion of the contract. However, there are a whole array of other contracts on swapping flats or residences in which the contracting parties are not witnesses in this trial, because I published in my book all the contracts that we managed to obtain, which is a testimony which refutes the allegations from the indictment. Whether my objective was to publicly disclose the names of protected witnesses and thereby intimidate them, Judges, you know that Serbia and Yugoslavia for nearly half a century were under the Communist dictatorship and the Communist Marsal Tito and his successors. This Communist regime put a ban, a judicial ban on seven of the books that I wrote. I have to reluctantly admit that the prosecutors in those trials against me had prepared themselves much thoroughly than this Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal has done. They had read all the books from cover to cover, and according to the practices then in place, did their job, but were -- they were much better prepared. We have here a Prosecutor who has no idea what this book contains. He is making arbitrary allegations that my intention was to disclose the names of protected witnesses and therefore intimidate them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Therefore, it was not my aim to intimidate and instil fear into protected witnesses or to make their names public. It was my aim to uncover the (redacted) was a construed one based on false accusations, on false statements, and that's what I've proved during the proceedings and trial against me. Not one stone has been left standing of any of the accusations or anything else, and that's why the whole trial has been blocked. And the Trial Chamber doesn't know how to deal with this problem and get out of this cul-de-sac, and they cannot acquit me, and they cannot act upon the requirements of the Prosecution. So it's checkmate. How long this will go on, I don't know. We'll see. And it's not important. I have patience myself, seven years and then another seven years. I can stay here another 70 years if need be. In this book, the Prosecutor says there were elements which can identify the protected witnesses. In principle, that is true, but you have lots of experience in the other trials that you have taken part in, gentlemen Judges, and in each of those trials it is possible, if it was in open session or public session, to identify a protected witness whose voice has been distorted, whose image has been distorted, who is testifying under a pseudonym, from the environment he comes from, on the basis of the subject to which he is testifying. Mr. Kwon at the time was the Judge in the Milosevic trial, for example. I don't think Mr. Bonomy was in the trial yet when Milan Babic testified as a protected witness. I followed the trial in Belgrade and immediately recognised Milan Babic on the basis of what he was saying in the courtroom. Several days later the protective measures were lifted and Milan Babic continued to testify in open session, publicly. So that is all possible by deduction and by using your intelligence. Experts, 20 years ago, established that my IQ was above 240. Perhaps these experts are telling lies. Now, how -- what's Mr. MacFarlane's IQ? I don't know. Before this trial I thought his IQ was much higher than I think it is now, but of course I don't want to say anything derogatory about anyone, because he has raised the question of intelligence and the capabilities of an average man, so that brings me to these associations without wishing to insult him. Now, who could have concluded who this was about when it came to three protected witnesses in reading this book? Well, ask yourselves, Who has had the time and put in the effort to read a book that is 1.200 pages long just to have the names of protected witnesses disclosed? That's not what you would have done. You print an anonymous flyer, an anonymous pamphlet and nobody knows who the author of it is, and you disclose the names and then you call in people to intimidate the witnesses, to instil fear. In Haradinaj, for example, protected witnesses were killed. In no Serb trial did you have anything of that kind. How many witnesses were killed in the Haradinaj case, ten? Dozens? Who knows? The Prosecutor goes on to say that this is a very serious problem in this case. That's just not true. It's absolutely not true. There is no problem here. All we have here is the Prosecutors thinking up this problem when they faced a fiasco in the main trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted) The book was being sold at these public promotions and was later distributed free of charge, and you can download any copy free of charge from my internet site, because I don't charge on my site. So a lot of time went by until this idea came to the Prosecutor that he should take some steps, and now the logical question arises of why is something being undertaken at precisely this point; whereas for a year and a half nothing was done about it, and now suddenly this has been brought up. The Prosecutor is facing a problem, and to find their way out of the problem they want to prevent me from defending myself and to impose counsel on me who would not represent my interests but would represent the interests of the Prosecutor and the USA, NATO, the European Union, and so on and so forth. That's the crux of the matter. And it is for that reason that the Prosecutor suddenly needed to proclaim me and have you proclaim me guilty here so that this would be a legal groundwork in order for them to be able to say that I have abused my right of self-representation in my own trial. It doesn't matter what the sanctions are. You have to agree with respect to the judgements that are meted out in the main trials. The sanctions for contempt of court are symbolic. For somebody who has been in prisoner already for seven years, they are even ludicrous. What do I care about the sanctions that you can impose against me? But what is essential and vital is that you proclaim me guilty so that then the Prosecutor can come out with a new request on the basis of your judgement, and it can say the Trial Chamber has established that I violated the protective rights of witnesses and therefore abused my role as defending myself, and so forfeited my right to continue to defend myself. That's what they want to achieve. And now when we come to the Defence case, when it's the turn of the Defence case, you would like to have me being represented by a Prosecution spy, whereas I should act as a cretin my own trial. There are very rare trials where the accused can take part in questioning of witnesses, and you know that better than me. The accused that makes the wrong decision and takes on counsel means that he's left his fate into the hands of others, and he can say good-bye to his future. All he can expect is how -- what sentence will be meted out to him in this ideal cooperation between the Prosecutor and Defence counsel. Well, not all Defence counsels are like that but most of them are because it is the Tribunal who pays for Defence counsel, not the accused. And so they're subject to the will of those people in the OTP, because what the Defence counsel are afraid of are being -- is being deprived of a job here. They're not interested in anything else. And another point is very important in these concerns. Mr. MacFarlane does not have a shred of evidence to show that any one of these three protected witnesses, after the publication of my book, had any kind of problems, that somebody provoked them, intimidated them, threatened them, or anything of the kind, took measures of physical assault against him or his family, their property, or whatever. None of that happened. And I'll tell you one more thing. All three, all three protected witnesses have already appeared in public several times. They have given interviews to papers where they presented similar things, just like what they said in their statements to the Prosecutor. So where's the problem then? Where's the intimidation, and why would I want to intimidate them in the first place, because I dealt with them very well here in the courtroom. I completely overturned their testimony. So why would I have the need to intimidate them? My arguments -- the force of my arguments was so strong that there was nothing left of the indictment, not a stone, and in private conversation, if they trust you, people will tell you that. Your colleagues from the Prosecution will tell you that, will own up to that. I'm quite sure of that, because there's public opinion within the Tribunal itself which is fully conscious of the fact that the OTP and the Prosecutor in my trial has experienced a complete fiasco, and now the trial is at a standstill and we're waiting for something. What we're waiting for, we're waiting for you to impose counsel on me so that then he can act in court instead of me, and of course everything would evolve quite differently then. Then the counsel would kow-tow to the Prosecutor and every false witness, and would to a maximum extent collaborate with the Prosecutor. You see, here Mr. MacFarlane claims that I wanted to hide something. I didn't want to hide anything. I didn't want to pull the wool over anything there. And in the study that my associates compiled, the identity of a protected witness is not disclosed anywhere. If you read the whole book and if you read it in -- paying great attention, and then if somebody were to draw your attention, somebody from outside to draw your attention to the fact that in the multitude of facts over 1.200 pages, there are three particular witnesses mentioned. Now, 1.200 pages is many more newspaper pages, which is 2.400 journalist pages. So only if somebody has indices in advance pointed out to him would he be able to come to the conclusions that Mr. MacFarlane has come to. Not everybody can do that. Not everybody would be in a position to do that. And I ask you, who is it that -- which reader can concentrate his efforts so much to be as concentrated from page 1 to all 1.200 pages? Only somebody with a great deal of experience. Not everybody is capable of reading in that form and applying their concentration that much. It's not a question of logical deduction and conclusion. It is a question of getting to grips with this vast material before you and to extract the portions that the Prosecutor wished to extract and point to. Now, since the Prosecutor has not read this book, other people have written down the gist of what could be important, and then that seems to be the backbone -- it would appear that this was the backbone of the book, the skeleton of the book, but that's not true either. All the incidents that took place in a certain location, it would appear, were taken to court in Serbia. Here material evidence is shown that false testimony was given to the OTP, because the man in statement two, the Prosecutor says one thing, whereas the court documents and files tell us something quite different. And it is these court files and court documents that are being presented here, whereas the Prosecutor has read none of it. Then the Prosecutor goes on to say that I would be satisfied in seeing that several thousand copies were downloaded from my site. Well, that's what every author would like to see, that his book is published in many, many copies, but the point is that this book is too expensive for me to print a new edition. The first edition was sold under cost price, or it was distributed free of charge. A second edition would be far too expensive. We can't distribute that many copies free of charge. And if somebody wants to read the book, they can download it from my site. And this was published in the Serbian Radical Party's site, and it has a party character. And the Serbian Radical Party, it is in its interests, in the interests of the Serbian Radical Party to prove to the public and to prove to a professional public opinion, to which these books are oriented in the first place, that one of the affairs that are mentioned in the indictment, the indictment raised against me as president of the Serbian Radical Party has been completely construed, artificially construed. And as I say, the Serbian Radical Party is the publisher of this book and I am the exclusive author of this book, and now people who acted upon my instructions acted strictly as I instructed them to do. Therefore, I'm responsible for each and every page to be found in this book. And there's no doubt about that, and we needn't have wasted time on matters of that kind at all. Well, now, the Prosecutor referred to my statement about people who are clever and who can understand. This is not only about cleverness. It's about professionalism. Only a person who understands some basic notions and categories can read this book. This book is not for general public. The man in the street can be fascinated by the cover of this book and the number of pages, but an ordinary person doesn't have enough patience to read the whole book. A lawyer who is particularly interested in this specific field will embark on reading this book, but this is a very small number of people. If my intention was to intimidate the witnesses, I would have instructed someone to write a pamphlet printed in 10 or 20 pages and distributed it around. Even the pamphlet could have contained an invitation to have these witnesses attacked or to have something undertaken. There was nothing like that with me. During the whole process none of this took place. But this is not the first time that The Hague Office of the Prosecution wanted to fabricate a trial against me for contempt of court. Let me remind you -- perhaps Judge Parker may remember this because he was then the president of the Chamber, that back in 2005 the OTP, based solely on one telephone conversation that I made in which I said to my friend in Serbia this: "I heard that so-and-so was a false, secret witness in some of the trial and that he is doing some job in your municipality. Please try to get rid of this," and things to that effect. Now, after the OTP had been informed by the detention administration, ordered a ban to be imposed on me in terms of all telephone calls and all visits, under suspicion that I had disclosed the name of a protected witness. For the full two months I had no contact with the world outside. I didn't receive a single visit from my family. My father-in-law died during that period, and also my sister-in-law's husband also died, and I had no contact with anyone. After the two months expired, the OTP decided not to pursue and to prosecute me for contempt of court, although they had claimed that this man was a protected witness in my case, and they had never informed me about this. You know when I was informed about this, that this man could appear as a witness in my case? Only recently, around the new year, never before that. I had never received his statement. There was no statement, for that matter, given by him. The first statement he gave to the OTP was in December last year, nearly three years after the event that I have just described. Yes, it is true that he had been interrogated as a suspect. I'm just telling you that this is an illustration of similar attempts by the OTP for me to be sentenced for contempt of court and therefore to deprive me of the right for -- to self-representation. That was their main driving force. After they had failed to achieve that, they resorted to some more brutal method, and you know how this ended in 2006 and how the whole Trial Chamber had to be replaced. There was another attempt on the part of the Prosecution to accuse me of contempt of court. I presume that Judge Parker will remember that as well, but I had no idea what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, how much would you need? How much longer do you need to conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would like us to have a break, we can take a break. I cannot give you an exact estimate, but I will go with your request. You tell me how much you need until the end, but I will of course not overstep the time allocated to the OTP. You please warn me if I have already overstepped the line, but if I'm given time, I would like to say a few things more. So if you think this is the time for the break, we can take a break, and after that, please tell me how much time you're going to give me. I will speak for as long as you grant me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and I'll -- I would like you to conclude after which -- to conclude in half an hour after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quite satisfied with half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break I started talking about another instance when the OTP tried to institute proceedings for contempt of court. That took place in 2005. But even today I have no idea on what this request had been based. When everything came to a close, the Trial Chamber, including Judge Parker, instructed the representative of the registry to inform me, in one sentence, that there had been a request by the Prosecution to institute proceedings for contempt of court and that the Trial Chamber had dismissed this question. Therefore, that was a third attempt on the part of the OTP to institute such proceedings with the sole purpose of creating artificially illegal basis for depriving me of the right to self-representation. I don't know, Judges, how much you are aware of the fact that many other forms of torture had been exercised and applied to me during the past seven years. Towards the end 2003 until July 2004, for seven months I was deprived, unlawfully, any telephone conversations or any contacts and visits by my family with the explanation that my political party had won a lot of votes in the election and that in these telephone conversations and through these visits I could influence the post-electoral situation in Serbia. Two days ago something totally incredible happened. The detention unit administration forbidden -- has forbidden me to go out for a stroll. That happened on the 27th, 28th and 29th of May. You know, Judges, that this is absolutely unacceptable and impermissible. Even those on a death row have a right to take a stroll for an hour or two. What happened? Two days ago when I went out for a walk in the courtyard that has no greenery in it, where there is no sunshine during wintertime, we have to pass the room for collective visits and two offices where lawyers are working. I saw another co-prisoner of mine, and I just shouted at him, "Hold on, general," and I mentioned his name. One of the supervisors of the guards in civilian clothes intervened and he got embroiled with me in a verbal argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm wondering what relevance this has to do with this case. Could you concentrate on this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is because I am focussed on this case and I think this has been devised in order to psychologically destabilise me before the trial. No one can destabilise me psychologically but those guys there obviously don't know that, because the new governor of the detention unit doesn't know that, and I had to tell you this story. You know, Judges, that no one can have his right to have a stroll be restricted. I know that I am the worst detainee in Scheveningen. I admit that I am the most undisciplined one, but you cannot impose a disciplinary measure such as the deprivation of the right to have a walk outside. This has been an unprecedented occurrence, and this happened only two days ago before this case, and it's up to you to decide why this happened and why this totally unlawful step was taken. Just a few more words about the Prosecution case. On several occasions, Mr. MacFarlane alleges that it seems that I had issued instructions. It seems I had made a conscientious decision to avoid the mentioning of the name of a witness. What does the term "it seems" mean in criminal law? Is that a serious statement? It seems that I have committed a crime, and based on that, I'm now on trial because that is what it seems. There is no such thing as "it seems" in the criminal law. You either have evidence or you don't have evidence when it comes to criminal law. The criminal law cannot tolerate any guesswork. The Prosecutor here is guessing all the time. Why? My impression is that he has a preconception in his mind that his case will be successful and therefore he can afford this luxury to himself to make a guesswork. A prosecutor who is not convinced in advance of the outcome of the proceedings will not allow such an approach. He will leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide, and he will rely on the professional assessment by the Chamber about his conduct in the courtroom. He also said that with my associate, I put together a -- a puzzle, a jigsaw puzzle, in order to avoid criminal proceedings. Now, I'm asking you, who in the whole wide world is capable of putting together such a complicated jigsaw puzzle? If you do it artificially, you can't make it. It cannot fit together. But when you put documents in a systematic fashion, put them together systematically, that are so convincing then it might look a work of genius or a work of art. In fact, this is not the case either. This is simply a very successful exposure of a plot and conspiracy, because everything that relates to this particular case is a conspiracy. You know, Judges, that these events that took place in this particular location, no one else, apart from me, has ever been charged for. How does that fit to the joint criminal enterprise and everything else? No one here can offer any answers to these questions. The Prosecutor went on to say that I was successful in putting together this jigsaw puzzle but that that had actually been my plan all along. It is obvious from the entire book that my sole plan was to unmask and expose this conspiracy. There is nothing in the book that indicates that my plan had been to intimidate the witnesses. There's another thing that struck me. I am intentionally avoiding to comment all the details from Mr. MacFarlane's case because simply I want to avoid going into private session, because I'm not interested in that. Of all the public principles that the civilised court in criminal proceedings adhere to is the principle of public access, because I rely on the principle that you are putting me on trial and the public is putting you on trial. Let me give you just one detail. In case and in his presentation, Mr. MacFarlane listed the methods that I used in order to reveal the identity of protected witnesses. Among other things, he alleges that I described one of these witnesses as a notorious alcoholic and thereby I revealed his identity. So this is possible again. Since I don't intend to use up the whole full hour that you allotted to me, I will conclude in this way in this case for contempt of court. The existence of any criminal offence or the substance of a crime has not been established in this case. The Prosecutor failed in every respect to prove mens rea, that is to say, my intent to reveal the names of the protected witnesses for the purpose of intimidating them. There is no such thing. It is now up to you to decide, either based on your conscience or other interests that you might have, this is your personal matter, and I said what I wanted to say to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if I understood you correctly, one of your submissions suggested that the three witnesses have given interviews to press on some occasion in terms similar to the statements to the Prosecution. What material is there to support that submission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are the newspaper interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you then able to submit to us in writing, after you return to the detention unit, copies of these newspaper interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we're in open session now, I can say publicly, or I can give instructions to my case manager, Marina Raguz, and my legal advisor in these proceedings, Dejan Mirovic, to supply me on Monday, or, rather, to supply to you on Monday -- to send by e-mail to the Registry photocopies of some of those interviews from the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, do you consider it necessary for you to respond to Mr. Seselj's submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it's necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber thanks the amicus Prosecutor, Mr. MacFarlane, and the accused for their submissions. We reserve our decision and take the case under our advisement and issue our decision, judgement, in due course. We rise. --- Where upon the Rule 77 Hearing adjourned at 6.19 p.m. 23 24 25
